summary: A buffer overflow happens when a program writes more data into a fixed-size buffer than it can hold, spilling into adjacent memory. On the stack this can overwrite saved registers and the return address, handing control to an attacker.

sections.heading: What goes wrong
sections.body: C does no bounds checking. Writing past the end of an array silently corrupts whatever sits next to it: other locals, a saved frame pointer, or the return address.

sections.heading: Stack-based vs heap-based
bullets: Stack-based: overflow a local buffer to reach the return address or function pointers. Most common and best understood.
Heap-based: overflow a heap block to corrupt allocator metadata or neighbouring objects. Harder, but real.

sections.heading: How stack smashing works
bullets: A call pushes the return address; the callee allocates locals below it.
Input longer than the buffer climbs upward over saved registers.
The attacker chooses bytes that overwrite the return address.
On `ret`, the CPU jumps to the attacker's chosen address.

sections.heading: Dangerous functions
bullets: `gets` (removed from C11), `strcpy`, `strcat`, `sprintf`, `scanf("%s")` do no length checking.
Safer: `fgets`, `snprintf`, `strncpy`/`strlcpy` (mind termination), `memcpy` with a verified length.

sections.heading: Defences
bullets: Stack canaries: a secret value before the return address, checked on return (`-fstack-protector`).
NX / DEP: stack and heap pages are not executable.
ASLR: randomize addresses so exploits cannot hard-code targets.

subtopics.title: Worked example: 5-byte buffer
subtopics.summary: Why 9 bytes can crash and 8 may not.

sections.body: Compilers pad stack buffers to the machine word. A `char buf[5]` may occupy 8 bytes, so 8 input bytes can seem fine while 9 clobber adjacent data and fault. The absence of a crash is not proof of safety; it is undefined behavior either way.
When the stack is non-executable, attackers chain short existing code snippets ('gadgets') ending in `ret`, built by controlling the stack. ASLR and CFI make this harder.
Writing `buf[n]` for a size-`n` array, or `printf(user_input)`, can be as exploitable as a large overflow. Always pass a constant format string.

AddressSanitizer reports stack and heap overflows at run time with a precise location. Valgrind finds heap overruns. Static analyzers and compiler warnings (`-Wall -Wextra -Warray-bounds`) catch many at build time.

takeaways: C will not stop you writing past a buffer; you must bound every copy.
Stack overflows can overwrite the return address and redirect execution.
Prefer length-aware APIs and verify sizes.
Layer defences: canaries, NX, ASLR, sanitizers.
